On a natural low hillock with good views in all directions. Large recumbent irregular shaped sandstone boulder (2.1m E-W x 1.3m N-S; T 0.4m avg.) resting on top of smaller stones which are embedded into the ground. Skeletal remains found underneath standing stone on its W side in 1935 (Duignan 1935). According to Stanley (1870-71, 27-9) the stone was erect (H 6ft) with evidence of packing stones at its base. Described by Stanley as 'There is a 'clug stucogh' on Mr. Belton's land in Ballynamona, near Durrow. It is a massive conglomerate, stands about six feet high, and has other sandstones gathered to its base to keep it steady (Stanley 1870-71, 28).

Test excavation was carried out by Dominic Delany under licence no. 00E0866 at the site of a proposed dwelling on 11 November, in response to a request for further information from Offaly County Council. The site lies c. 1km south-east of the archaeological complex at Croghan Hill and is within the area of constraint around the possible site of a standing stone. The stone stood c. 50m east of the proposed dwelling and, according to local information, now lies buried in the field in which it formerly stood. A second standing stone (SMR 10:14) lies c. 100m south-west of the site. Four test-trenches were excavated on the footprint of the proposed development. The topsoil, 0.7m thick, directly overlay bedrock and natural sand and gravel deposits. No archaeological material was discovered.

OF016-016----:
Unable to locate stone known locally as 'Barna Liaga stone'. Local information indicated that it was a large stone lying flat on the ground. They never remembered it standing erect. In the area where the stone is located there was a lot of field clearance in the ditch. The stone may have been removed during such field clearance. Described by Stanley (1870-1, 27-9) as the 'Barna Liaga' stone which was once erect and measured 6ft by 6ft and 3ft thick.
Thlmas Stanley recorded in the nineteenth century that 'The stone 'Barna Liaga' is on the edge of a forgotten road, and it is about midway between the castle of Ballycowen and the castle upon Counsellor Molloys farm in Ballykilmurry. Betty Larkin told me she remembered to sit on its top before it was turned on its side. It is a sandstone. The upper surface measures nigh six feet every way, and it is about half that measure in thickness' (JRSAI 187-1, 28).

OF039-065----:
Visited by Seán Ó Nualláin in 1966 in response to report of a 'Dolmen' and 'Grave' in Ballywilliam Wood. The 'Grave' lies 20m SW of the 'Dolmen' (OF039-030----) at the eastern edge of Ballywilliam Wood. S Ó Nualláin stated that the 'Grave' may be an artificial (or partly artificial) structure and that excavation would be necessary to establish its true nature. Visited by E. Cody on 16 August 1995. It is clear that this is an artificial structure of a megalithic nature and may well be a megalithic tomb. Plan of monument in Megalithic Survey field book for Offaly/Kildare/Laois.
Information from E. Cody, 26 January 2010.
Compiled by Caimin O'Brien

OF044-014----:
The monument stands in a copse at the southern edge of a stretch of lowlying, marshy land and is overlooked from the S by higher ground. The surviving remains indicate the presence of a rectangular chamber deeply buried at the approximate centre of a substantial, subcircular, stony mound (diam. 11-12m; H 0.8m). The chamber (L 3.3m; Wth 1.5m), aligned roughly ESE-WNW, is represented by four set stones. An inward-leaning, somewhat gable-topped example marks the ESE end of the structure while a stone on the more northerly side of the chamber adjoins one end of the last, and another on the southern side which leans inwards, adjoins its opposite end. A second stone on the S side, just over 1m to the W, is taller than the other set stones. A large and now dislodged roofstone (L 3.2m; max. Wth 2.8m; T 0.3m) partly overlies the western end of the chamber. Another large stone lying prostrate and broken underneath the roofstone may have formed part of the structure as also may some of the sizable slabs lying on the mound.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Offaly' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 13 January 2010
